title: TSMC’s September sales surge year-over-year as AI drives chip demand
content: The world's largest contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co posted revenue of $511.86 billion New Taiwan dollars ($16.03 billion) for September, up 54.6% on the year prior, but down 0.6% on August . Its third quarter revenue came around $NT1.49 trillion. The company closed 1.35% lower ahead of releasing monthly figures. TSMC, which counts Nvidia and Apple among its customers, has been a major beneficiary of surging demand for advanced AI chips. In September, TSMC committed to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key technology for producing more advanced chips, joining Samsung Electronics among customers adopting the technology. It is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings next week. Correction: The story has been updated to reflect that sales did not hit a record high in September.

title: Trump awarding medals to Musk, Dell, Nadella and other tech execs at science summit
content: President Donald Trump is awarding medals to a number of leading tech executives, including Elon Musk and Michael Dell , at a science summit on Thursday, CNBC has confirmed. Musk, who leads SpaceX and Tesla , is receiving the National Medal of Science, as are Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, according to the White House. Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be given the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The event is titled Science: A New Golden Age Summit. Fox News was first to report on it. "The Trump Administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology," Liz Huston, White House assistant press secretary said, in an emailed statement. "These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation." The summit comes a little over a week after Trump hosted a lunch at the White House focused on artificial intelligence that included several of those executives and many others in the industry. Trump told reporters after the gathering that he signed a "morally binding" document with the tech leaders, as calls for a slowdown in the development of AI models reached a fever pitch. Each of the awards recipients at Thursday's summit has financially contributed, in some capacity, to President Trump or Republican campaigns and causes. Musk was Trump's biggest financial backer in the 2024 election cycle, contributing over $290 million, and then led an effort to slash the federal workforce as a special government employee of the Trump administration. Brin attended Trump's inauguration and contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Republican National Committee in 2025. Huang donated to a fund to build Trump's White House ballroom, and Nvidia contributed $1 million to Trump's inauguration ceremony. Dell is a longtime Trump donor. Along with his wife Susan, he committed $6.25 billion to seed Trump Accounts designed to jumpstart savings for children in the U.S. AMD is also contributing to Trump funds. According to his most recent disclosure, Trump bought or sold shares in SpaceX, Tesla, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD and Google parent Alphabet as recently as July . — CNBC's Eamon Javers contributed to this report. title: FCC to vote on auctioning 25MHz of 'prime spectrum' in move that could benefit Amazon, SpaceX
content: The Federal Communications Commission said Wednesday it will vote on a proposal to auction 25 megahertz of "prime spectrum" to support "direct-to-device" services from satellites to smart phones. The FCC, in a press release, also said it would vote Oct. 29 on taking public comment on a proposal to make an additional 482MHz of spectrum available for supplemental coverage from space and to modernize FCC rules for D2D services in the licensed spectrum. The two proposals could benefit companies such as SpaceX and Amazon , which have moved to expand D2D services with satellite networks. A third proposal to be voted on "would eliminate an outdated restriction that prevents drone operations in the 800 MHz Cellular band," the FCC said. Amazon in July asked the FCC to approve the company launching up to 5,105 internet satellites as part of a constellation to provide direct-to-device connectivity. Amazon, in a filing that month, said it was targeting users who are "unserved or underserved" by existing wireless providers. In August, Amazon said it would acquire Globalstar in a deal worth more than $11.5 billion to boost Amazon's Leo satellite internet business. On Tuesday, the FCC's Space Bureau granted an application for SpaceX's new direct-to-cell system of 15,000 satellites. "This constellation will use the spectrum SpaceX purchased from EchoStar earlier this year, which the FCC approved in a major win for the American space economy," the FCC said in the Wednesday press release. "The 'direct-to-device' proposals work to continue leveraging this cutting-edge tech to end cell phone dead zones and provide service directly from next-gen satellite constellations to your smartphone," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, said in a statement Wednesday. "And our final rules on drones further President Trump's call for drone dominance, providing the emerging American drone economy with usable spectrum to support the next generation of commercial and defense innovations."

title: Microsoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip
content: Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices. The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post . While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud. Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics. "Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement. Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT. Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey . This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices. In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said. The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event. A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access. Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software. Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving. "I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true." WATCH: Microsoft unveils Muse for Windows

An analysis of roughly 500 spear points suggests that inherited knowledge of stone deposits helped Ice Age hunters decide which tools were worth carrying. Ice Age hunters in the Tennessee River Valley sometimes threw away stone spearheads that were still usable. Leaving a point behind lightened the load, but replacing it required suitable rock, something people entering unfamiliar territory could not necessarily count on finding. “When you think about a people who are moving around a lot, understand that they didn’t have any pack animals,” said Shane Miller, an assistant professor of anthropology at the University of Alabama. “That puts limitations on what tools you discard and what you carry around. “You really don’t want to be carrying around a bag of rocks, and so you’re going to be judicious about balancing what you need versus what you can carry.” Miller and Jesse Tune, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of Mississippi and director of its Center for Archaeological Research, examined roughly 500 spear points recovered from the Tennessee River Valley. Their study, published in the Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory , compared tools left by Clovis and Cumberland groups to investigate how knowledge of local resources might have influenced what their owners kept. “How did they adapt to a place no one has ever been before?” Miller said. “We can’t interview these people, so we have to look at the things they left behind. “There aren’t that many archaeological sites for these people that we can dig, but what we have instead are lots and lots of points that people have found in this region.” Clovis groups were living in the Tennessee River Valley around 13,200 years ago , placing them among its earliest known inhabitants. Entering unfamiliar terrain meant having to locate the materials needed for daily life, including chert, a sedimentary rock well suited to making stone weapons. Skill at shaping a spearhead could only go so far without knowing where to obtain the stone. “Think about space exploration,” Tune said. “There really is no difference between Ice Age hunter-gatherers and the people sending missions and rovers to Mars. We’re moving into an area, deciding what to take with us, learning the resources, and slowly expanding. It’s the exact same process. “What we learn and how we pass on that knowledge are the same things that we’re still dealing with today. The only thing that’s changed is the technology.” Tune and Miller found that Clovis hunters were more likely to resharpen their spearheads than the later Cumberland groups. Keeping an existing point in use postponed the need to replace it, a pattern the researchers interpret as a possible way of conserving resources when hunters were less certain where to find more stone. “We hang on to stuff today, but when we’re talking about mobile hunter-gatherers, they had a different understanding and worldview when it came to personal possessions,” Tune said. “Spear points were designed to be disposable objects, and that makes what the Clovis were doing interesting.” Hunters followed seasons, rivers, and game across the Americas, carrying tools that now survive as some of the few traces of their daily lives. The researchers are using those objects to reconstruct decisions made in surroundings very different from the valley today. “We’re talking about Ice Age hunter-gatherers, people that looked and acted just like us and had the same needs that we do,” Tune said. “But they’re living in a world that is dominated by mastodons, mammoths, giant sloths – all these animals that are totally unfamiliar to us today. “What we’re looking at – the points – is a tiny part of their life, but we’re trying to see the rest of their behaviors through the lens of these spear points because that’s what we have.” Cumberland hunters followed the Clovis groups several hundred years later, leaving behind tools that gave Tune and Miller a different set of choices to examine. “When we look at the Cumberland points, we can see where they got the raw material, roughly the time period that they lived and that they’ve used the point multiple times,” Tune said. “But (the point) was rarely completely broken to the point that it couldn’t be used anymore. “So how did it end up in what was essentially the trash, and then in the archaeological record?” Cumberland hunters, the researchers suggest, inherited their predecessors’ knowledge of chert deposits and other resources. A usable spearhead left behind in the Tennessee River Valley may record the practical value of that inheritance: knowing where to find fresh stone made an old point easier to let go. Reference: “Foraging Theory and the Colonization of Unfamiliar Landscapes: Assessing Late Pleistocene Projectile Point Reduction Strategies” by Jesse W. Tune, and D. Shane Miller, 27 August 2026, Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory . DOI: 10.1007/s10816-026-09825-w Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has died
content: Margaret Hamilton, the groundbreaking researcher who helped create the field of software engineering and whose code helped land NASA’s Apollo astronauts on the moon to win the 20th century space race, has died. She was 90. Hamilton’s former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, confirmed her death in a post from the department of aeronautics and astronautics. She died September 30, MIT reported. The cause of her death was not disclosed. It was during her time working at MIT, where she took a job in 1959 and remained until the mid-1970s, that Hamilton managed the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory. The division landed a contract with NASA in 1961. She ultimately led a team of 100 engineers that designed the software to guide NASA’s Apollo missions. Through her work, Hamilton is also credited as one of the founders of the field of software engineering — a term she popularized — by helping to establish it as a professional practice. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” Hamilton was honored in 2016 with the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama for her contribution to science and space travel. Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, according to MIT, and studied at the University of Michigan before receiving her degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Indiana. She took a job at MIT while her husband studied law at Harvard. While working to develop critical onboard software for the spacecraft — both command modules and lunar landers — that completed NASA’s historic Apollo flights — Hamilton is credited with making the system more robust and accident-resistant. One oft-cited failsafe she introduced was “the Lauren error,” according to MIT, which was named for her daughter and discovered when the then-4-year-old was fiddling with an Apollo command module simulator. “She liked to play astronaut because she saw me playing that way in certain simulations we would run,” Hamilton later recalled in an oral history project. “This was in a hardware simulation because we wanted to try how the software worked with all the other things — the astronaut, the hardware. So I remember one time when Lauren’s simulation crashed and I thought, ‘Oh my god, how did that happen?’’’ So, Hamilton programmed backstops to prevent an astronaut from running into the same problem mid-flight, an issue that would have yielded far more dire consequences in space. NASA pointed to one notable example where Hamilton’s work helped ensure mission success: During the famed 1969 Apollo 11 mission, Hamilton’s software overrode an errant attempt to swap the flight computer’s primary processing to a radar system. The software’s intervention, which occurred just three minutes before the first ever touchdown on the lunar surface, “permitted the mission to safely continue,” NASA said . After its work on Apollo, the MIT Instrumentation Lab spun off to become the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, now known as Draper Laboratory . Hamilton did not join the company, setting off instead to form her own company, but Draper’s CEO, Jerry Wohletz, said in a statement in MIT’s Wednesday announcement that Hamilton left an “indelible mark.” “Through her leadership and contributions,” Wohletz said, “she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.” In 2003, Hamilton was also awarded NASA’s Exceptional Space Act Award. The technologist who nominated Hamilton for the honor, Paul Curto, said at the time, “I was surprised to discover she was never formally recognized for her groundbreaking work.” “Her concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling, end-to-end testing, and man-in-the-loop decision capability, such as priority displays, became the foundation for ultra-reliable software design,” he said.

title: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai awarded the Nobel Prize in chemistry for unraveling mystery of mirror molecules
content: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry for designing revolutionary experiments that replicated chemical asymmetry, a feat only previously seen in nature. Their work has solved one of the field’s enduring mysteries and advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing, the award committee said during a news conference on Wednesday at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. The pair’s work hinges on the concept of chirality: that the structure of molecules fundamental to life includes mirror image forms, a little like our hands. However, only one of those variants is actually found in the cells of living things. This phenomenon, known as homochirality, has long puzzled scientists because for years they weren’t able to replicate it in a lab, where chemical reactions usually created a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules. “Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, in a statement. In the early 1980s, French chemist Kagan found ways to control chemical reactions with different types of catalysts, allowing scientists to produce a greater excess of one of the mirror image molecules. Soai, a Japanese scientist based at Tokyo University of Science, then built on this work by designing a chemical reaction in which only one of two possible images was formed. “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat,” the Nobel committee noted. Receiving the Nobel Prize marked “one of the most exciting days” in his life, Soai said in a telephone interview during the award presentation. He revealed he had been “out shopping” when he received the call telling him he had won. The Nobel committee said at the news conference that it hadn’t immediately been able to get hold of Kagan. The duo’s research has both given chemists fundamental new tools that are widely used in their daily work and awakened interest in the chemistry of life’s origins, the committee said. Phillip Broadwith, the business editor at Chemistry World, which is published by the Royal Society of Chemistry, said Kagan’s and Soai’s achievement allowed scientists to choose which mirror image of a molecule to make, a capability which is crucial for manufacturing things like drugs or even flavors and fragrances. “It also helps to explain a possible way that all the chiral molecules on Earth – our proteins, sugars and biomolecules, settled into one specific handedness rather than the other, so it’s fascinating science,” he added. Last year’s prize was awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for developing “metal-organic frameworks,” a form of molecular architecture that packs vast amounts of space into tiny structures – which the committee likened to Hermione Granger’s magical handbag in the “Harry Potter” novel series. Kagan and Soai share the 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) chemistry prize announced on Wednesday - the third award announced this week. On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded to a trio of scientists for their work developing a technique to decode the inner workings of the brain. On Tuesday, the physics prize went to Francis Halzen, a pioneering Belgian astrophysicist whose work developing a massive observatory in Antarctica to detect “ghostly” cosmic particles laid the foundations for “an entirely new type of astronomy,” the committee said. The literature and peace prizes will be announced on Thursday and Friday, respectively, followed by the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on October 12. This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.

title: MP criticises US tech firm over fake images no show
content:
A Suffolk MP has criticised a US tech firm after its no show at a New York City Council meeting to discuss putting in laws to regulate AI developers.
Jess Asato is suing xAI in the UK after sexualised images of her were created by its AI chatbot tool, Grok.
She is seeking damages from the company, owned by Elon Musk, for the misuse of her private information and breaches of data protection rules.
Asato told the BBC that the failure of SpaceXAI - which owns xAI - to turn up at the hearing, despite being subpoenaed, demonstrated its "level of arrogance". SpaceXAI has been contacted for comment.
The hearing, which was held on 5 October, was the council's Committee of the Whole - a rare meeting where all council members are present.
In her opening statement, the speaker, Julie Menin, acknowledged the benefit of AI use on science and medical breakthroughs, but said the meeting had been called in response to "serious existential safety concerns" over AI development and "the catastrophic dangers of the technology".
She added that the lack of federal regulation of AI developers in the USA had meant they needed to develop effective AI regulation in New York.
In America, national laws are made by federal government - but states and cities can also make their own legislation.
After being invited to speak about her experiences and legal action, Asato said: "It was quite a long way to go but I thought if I could take the message of what we're trying to do here in the UK over to New York, to the centre of AI and tech development, then I might be able to help to get a much safer platform built for the future."
She said her flight and accommodation had been paid for by Reset Tech, a public policy organisation advocating for technology that protects children, consumers, and public safety.
Asato filed a lawsuit back in July , suing xAI for damages after non-consensual images and videos, including some showing her being sexually assaulted, were shared online.
She is seeking damages for the misuse of her private information and breaches of data protection rules, as well as a court order requiring the company to find and remove any remaining online images.
xAI is yet to file a defence to the legal action.
Asato said she also highlighted in her evidence that women were disproportionally affected.
She said: "We know that 99% of images that are made into sexualised videos are of women. 90% of deep fake pornographic images are of women, so it's a very gendered crime.
"They also specifically asked me about elected representatives, because obviously I am a member of parliament, and I talked about the fact that we also know that women are 33 times more likely to be targeted by sexual deep fakes than men who are elected.
"So it is definitely something that we can see right across the piece, whether you're elected or not. Women are targeted by deep fake AI."
At the hearing, the five major AI developers in New York - Anthropic, Meta, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI - were subpoenaed to testify.
Four of them turned up but SpaceXAI did not send a representative.
Asato said: "I think it shows a certain amount of arrogance or a sense that actually  these companies don't need to be held accountable by elected representatives."

title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
content:
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens , it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.

title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
content: Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters. The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work. However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope. "It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC. The UK was once home to large tuna fisheries, but overfishing of both the tuna and the smaller fish it preys on meant that by the 1960s it had largely disappeared. The report credits its recent recovery to a concerted international effort that included reducing catch quotas, size limits and protection of spawning grounds, which was backed by campaigns from consumers, chefs and retailers. Hannah Rudd, head of marine at the Angling Trust, said the result of this effort was close to an "explosion" in the population of the species. "I think bluefin tuna is a golden case study that fisheries management works," she said. The WWF report highlighted other species recoveries around the world, including an increase of more than 70% in the number of wild tigers - from around 3,200 in 2010 to about 5,700 in 2025. Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to have its protection status downgraded from "endangered" to "least concern", after 50 years of conservation work in about 80 countries. Elephant numbers are stable or growing in parts of southern Africa, thanks in part to new laws that give local people a share of the income elephants bring, including tourism. Barrett said these successes resulted from a clear goal with a credible plan and people who believed they could make a difference. The report calls it "the science of hope". "Hope is not the same thing as wishful thinking," he said. "Hope is not passive. Hope's about action." But despite the individual successes, the overall picture for nature remains stark. Working with the Zoological Society of London, WWF tracks nearly 36,000 populations of almost 6,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. It estimates global monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The figure measures the average change in the size of those populations, not the number of animals lost. About half of the populations are stable or growing, but their gains are outweighed by losses elsewhere. Dr Katie Collins, a senior curator at the Natural History Museum in London, also said the index misses out vast numbers of important species because it covers only vertebrates, missing plants, insects and other creatures they depend on. "If you lose garden snails, you lose the song thrush," she warned. WWF says conservation alone cannot reverse the decline but there must be efforts to tackle the causes. The biggest pressures come from farming, which can destroy the habitats wildlife depends on, and burning fossil fuels for energy, which drives climate change. The organisation says the money is flowing the wrong way. In 2023, about $7.3 trillion (£5.53tn) went into activities that harm nature, compared with $220bn spent protecting or restoring it, the report estimates – a ratio of roughly 33 to one. Barrett has worked on seven Living Planet reports, but he said this was the first where the takeaway message was to focus on hope. "The fact that the science is still telling us that we've got a way out is actually extraordinary," he said. "So it's a closing window of opportunity, but it's still open, just, if we act now."
